title: Severe upper abdominal pain in a 38-year-old man
opening_brief:
You are a medical student in the emergency department.

A 38-year-old man has come in with severe upper abdominal pain that began last night.

Assess him, decide what you need to know, choose your investigations, and be ready to justify your differential.

patient.name: Vikram Sethi
patient.background: Unmarried, lives alone. Frequent work dinners.

persona.speech_style: In pain, speaks in short bursts, leans forward while sitting.
knows_not: how much alcohol counts as 'a lot'
quirks: Downplays his drinking at first; gives a fuller answer only if asked directly and non-judgementally.

chief_complaint: severe pain in the upper abdomen since last night

present_illness.onset: Came on over about an hour last night, a few hours after a party.
present_illness.site: Upper part of the stomach, in the middle and slightly to the left.
present_illness.character: Constant, boring, deep pain. Not colicky.
present_illness.radiation: Goes straight through to the back.
present_illness.duration: About 14 hours now, has not let up at all.
present_illness.severity: 9 out of 10, the worst pain he has had.
present_illness.aggravating: Lying flat makes it much worse. Any attempt to eat or drink makes it worse.
present_illness.relieving: Sitting up and leaning forward helps a little.
associated: vomited six or seven times, mostly bile, no relief after vomiting
has not passed stool since yesterday
present_illness.progression: Unchanged in severity, but the bloating is increasing.

past_medical: Two similar but much milder episodes in the last two years, each settled in a day
High triglycerides mentioned at a company health check, never treated
family: No family history of pancreatic disease
social: Drinks nearly every day; about a quarter bottle of whisky on weekdays and more at weekends, for the last ten years
Drank heavily at a party the night this started
review_of_systems_negative: no recent injury to the abdomen

examination.label: Vital signs
examination.result: Temperature 38.2 C. Pulse 118/min. BP 98/62 mmHg lying, 84/56 on sitting up. Respiratory rate 24/min. SpO2 95% on room air.

examination.label: General examination
examination.result: Ill-looking, dry mucous membranes, sitting forward. Mild scleral icterus. No pallor, no clubbing, no asterixis.

examination.label: Abdominal examination
examination.result: Distended, tender in the epigastrium with voluntary guarding. No board-like rigidity. Bowel sounds sluggish. No mass palpable. Liver and spleen not enlarged. No shifting dullness.

examination.label: Murphy's sign
examination.result: Negative. Right hypochondrial tenderness is much less than epigastric tenderness.

examination.label: Respiratory examination
examination.result: Reduced air entry at the left base with dullness. Right lung clear.

examination.label: Cardiovascular examination
examination.result: Tachycardic, heart sounds normal, no murmur. JVP low.

examination.label: Hernial orifices and per-rectal examination
examination.result: Hernial orifices free. Rectum empty, no melaena, no mass.

investigations.label: Liver function tests
investigations.result: Total bilirubin 2.4 mg/dL, direct 1.3. ALT 78 U/L, AST 96 U/L, ALP 156 U/L, GGT 288 U/L. Albumin 3.2 g/dL.

investigations.label: Renal function and electrolytes
investigations.result: Urea 58 mg/dL, creatinine 1.6 mg/dL. Na 132, K 3.9 mEq/L. Corrected calcium 7.6 mg/dL.

investigations.label: Serum triglycerides
investigations.result: Triglycerides 340 mg/dL (not in the range that causes pancreatitis on its own).

investigations.label: C-reactive protein
investigations.result: CRP 186 mg/L at 24 hours from onset.

investigations.label: Ultrasound abdomen
investigations.result: Bulky, hypoechoic pancreas with peripancreatic fluid. Gallbladder contains no calculi; wall not thickened. Common bile duct 4 mm, not dilated. Small left pleural effusion.

investigations.label: Erect chest X-ray
investigations.result: No free gas under the diaphragm. Small left pleural effusion. Lung fields otherwise clear.

investigations.label: 12-lead ECG
investigations.result: Sinus tachycardia at 116/min. No ST-segment or T-wave changes.

investigations.label: Contrast-enhanced CT abdomen
investigations.result: Diffusely enlarged oedematous pancreas with peripancreatic fat stranding and fluid. No necrosis identified at this stage.
investigations.note: CT within the first 72 hours understates necrosis and is not needed when the diagnosis is already established biochemically. Reserve it for deterioration or diagnostic doubt.

investigations.label: Upper GI endoscopy
investigations.result: Not performed in the acute phase.
investigations.note: Contraindicated as a first step in an acute abdomen.

differentials.why: Constant boring epigastric pain radiating to the back, relieved by leaning forward, after a heavy alcohol binge, with lipase more than three times the upper limit and a bulky pancreas on ultrasound.

The other cause of sudden severe epigastric pain with an unwell patient. Excluded by the absence of board-like rigidity and of free gas under the diaphragm — but it requires a surgical referral if suspected.
Inferior infarction classically presents as epigastric pain with vomiting. Excluded here by a normal ECG, but the ECG must actually be done.
Mother has gallstones and the bilirubin is mildly raised, but the pain is epigastric rather than right hypochondrial, Murphy's sign is negative and there are no calculi on ultrasound.
Pain out of proportion to signs fits, but the age, the absence of vascular risk factors and the biochemical picture make it unlikely.
Does not cause shock, a lipase of 1,840 or peripancreatic fluid.

final_diagnosis: Acute alcohol-induced pancreatitis with early organ dysfunction (hypotension, acute kidney injury, hypocalcaemia) and a left pleural effusion — a severe attack requiring aggressive fluid resuscitation and high-dependency monitoring
diagnosis_reasoning: Two of the three diagnostic criteria are met and the third is supportive: characteristic epigastric pain radiating to the back and relieved by leaning forward, lipase more than three times the upper limit of normal, and a bulky oedematous pancreas with peripancreatic fluid on ultrasound. The precipitant is a heavy alcohol binge on ten years of daily drinking, with a raised GGT and no gallstones. Postural hypotension, haematocrit 49%, creatinine 1.6 and corrected calcium 7.6 mark this as severe rather than mild.

history.label: Site of the pain
history.teaching_note: Epigastric localisation immediately narrows the differential.

history.label: Radiation to the back
history.teaching_note: Radiation straight through to the back is characteristic of retroperitoneal structures — pancreas and aorta.

history.label: Effect of posture on the pain
history.teaching_note: Relief on leaning forward is close to specific for pancreatic pain and is almost always missed by students.

history.label: Alcohol history, quantified
history.teaching_note: Alcohol and gallstones cause 80% of acute pancreatitis. Asking 'do you drink?' is not enough — quantity, frequency and duration all matter.

history.label: Vomiting and its character
history.teaching_note: Vomiting without relief of pain distinguishes pancreatitis from obstruction.

history.label: Previous similar episodes
history.teaching_note: Recurrent milder attacks suggest ongoing insult and possible chronic pancreatitis.

history.label: Gallstones and fatty-food intolerance
history.teaching_note: Gallstone pancreatitis needs a completely different pathway — early ERCP if there is cholangitis or obstruction.

history.label: Triglycerides and metabolic history
history.teaching_note: Hypertriglyceridaemia is the third commonest cause and is treatable.

history.label: Drug history including recent new medication
history.teaching_note: Azathioprine, valproate, thiazides and others cause drug-induced pancreatitis.

history.label: Bowel habit and passage of flatus
history.teaching_note: Absolute constipation with distension would point towards obstruction or ileus.

history.label: Urine output
history.teaching_note: Oliguria is an early marker of severity and of inadequate resuscitation.

examination.label: Vital signs including postural blood pressure
examination.teaching_note: Postural hypotension here signals substantial third-space fluid loss and drives resuscitation.

examination.label: Abdominal examination
examination.teaching_note: Guarding without board-like rigidity separates pancreatitis from perforation at the bedside.

examination.label: Hydration and general examination
examination.teaching_note: Clinical dehydration corroborates the haematocrit of 49%.

examination.label: Respiratory examination
examination.teaching_note: A left pleural effusion is a recognised early sign of severe pancreatitis.

examination.label: Flank and periumbilical discoloration
examination.teaching_note: Rare and late, but worth knowing and looking for.

investigations.label: Serum lipase or amylase
investigations.teaching_note: Lipase is more sensitive and stays elevated longer; a value over three times the upper limit is diagnostic in the right clinical context.

investigations.label: Ultrasound abdomen
investigations.teaching_note: The point of the ultrasound is to look for gallstones and duct dilatation, because that changes management, not to confirm the pancreatitis.

investigations.label: Renal function, electrolytes and calcium
investigations.teaching_note: Creatinine and calcium are severity markers and feed directly into scoring systems.

investigations.label: Complete blood count with haematocrit
investigations.teaching_note: A haematocrit above 44% that fails to fall with fluids predicts necrosis.

investigations.label: Liver function tests
investigations.teaching_note: An ALT above 150 U/L makes a gallstone aetiology far more likely; GGT points to alcohol.

investigations.label: Erect chest X-ray
investigations.teaching_note: The bedside test that excludes perforation, which is the surgical mimic.

investigations.label: ECG
investigations.teaching_note: Epigastric pain with vomiting can be an inferior myocardial infarction. Missing this is a classic and dangerous error.

investigations.label: Blood glucose
investigations.teaching_note: Hyperglycaemia is a severity marker in most scoring systems.

investigations.label: C-reactive protein
investigations.teaching_note: CRP above 150 mg/L at 48 hours predicts severe disease.

investigations.label: Serum triglycerides
investigations.teaching_note: Needed to identify or exclude hypertriglyceridaemic pancreatitis.

hints: Ask yourself what the patient's posture is telling you, and re-read what he said about lying flat.
Retroperitoneal structures produce pain that bores through to the back. Which one sits in the epigastrium, and what would have provoked it the night before?
Review the causes of severe constant epigastric pain that bores through to the back, and the single biochemical test that separates them. Then read how severity is judged in the first 24 hours.
teaching_points: Acute pancreatitis is diagnosed when two of three are present: characteristic pain, lipase or amylase above three times the upper limit, and characteristic imaging.
The first ultrasound is for gallstones, not for the pancreas — because a gallstone aetiology changes management.
Do not order a CT in the first 72 hours unless the diagnosis is in doubt or the patient deteriorates; it understates necrosis and delays fluids.
Severity is judged by organ dysfunction and haemoconcentration, not by the height of the amylase.
Always do an ECG in epigastric pain with vomiting — inferior myocardial infarction is the mimic that kills.
